note: Order follows the biblical text. Dates are approximate labels, not a scale.

events.t: In the beginning was the Word
events.sum: John starts before creation itself: the Word already existed, was with God, and was God, and everything was made through Him.

events.t: In the beginning was the Word
events.sum: Before anything was made, the Word already was. He did not begin.
The Word was in the closest relationship with God, distinct from Him yet face to face.
John says the Word is fully God. In verse 14 the Word becomes flesh.

events.t: All things were made through Him
events.sum: Nothing that exists came into being apart from the Word.
God speaks the world into order over six days and rests on the seventh. Christians read the days in different ways, but the text gives their order.
God says, "Let there be light," and separates light from darkness.
God makes an expanse to separate the waters above from the waters below.
The waters gather, dry land appears, and plants and trees grow.
God sets lights in the sky to mark days, seasons and years.
The waters fill with living creatures and birds fill the sky.
God makes land animals, then men and women in His own image, and calls it all very good.
God finishes His work, blesses the seventh day and makes it holy.
God forms the man from the dust, plants a garden, and gives him a wife.
Adam and Eve eat the forbidden fruit. Sin and death enter the world, with God's promise of a coming rescuer.
Cain kills his brother Abel out of jealousy, the first murder.
Because of widespread violence, God sends a flood. Noah's family and the animals are saved in the ark, and God sets a rainbow as His promise.
People try to build a city and tower to make a name for themselves. God confuses their language and scatters them.
God tells Abraham to leave home and promises to make him a great nation and bless all peoples through him.
God promises Abraham a son, a land and countless descendants, and gives circumcision as the sign.

events.t: Isaac is born and Abraham is tested
events.sum: Isaac is born to Abraham and Sarah in their old age. God later tests Abraham and provides a ram in Isaac's place.
Jacob is renamed Israel, and his twelve sons become the ancestors of the twelve tribes.

events.t: Joseph is sold into Egypt and rises
events.sum: Sold by his brothers, Joseph becomes ruler under Pharaoh and saves his family from famine. Jacob's family settles in Egypt.
A new Pharaoh forces the growing Israelite people into slave labor.
God calls Moses to lead Israel out of Egypt.

events.t: The ten plagues and the first Passover
events.sum: After ten plagues, Israel marks its doorposts with lamb's blood and the angel of death passes over.
Israel leaves Egypt, crosses the Red Sea on dry ground, and sees Pharaoh's army destroyed. Scholars place this around 1446 BC or around 1260 BC.
God gives Israel the Ten Commandments and makes His covenant with the nation.
Israel builds the portable tent where God's presence dwells among them.
Israel refuses to enter the land out of fear, and wanders for forty years.
Moses gives final words to Israel, names Joshua his successor, and dies within sight of the land.

events.t: Joshua crosses the Jordan; Jericho falls
events.sum: Israel enters Canaan and the walls of Jericho fall.

events.t: The land is divided among the tribes
events.sum: Each tribe receives its territory.
Israel repeats a cycle of turning from God, trouble, and rescue by leaders like Deborah, Gideon and Samson.

events.d: In the time of the Judges
events.sum: A Moabite widow stays loyal to Naomi and marries Boaz, becoming David's great-grandmother.
Samuel is dedicated to God as a boy and becomes prophet and judge. Israel asks for a king.
Samuel anoints Saul. His reign begins well but he disobeys God.
The young shepherd David defeats the giant Goliath with a sling and stone.
David unites the tribes, captures Jerusalem and makes it his capital. God promises that his throne will last.
God promises David a house and a kingdom that will have no end, which the New Testament links to Jesus.
Many Psalms are credited to David, and Proverbs and Ecclesiastes are traditionally linked to Solomon.
Solomon builds the Temple in Jerusalem, and God's glory fills it.
After Solomon, ten northern tribes follow Jeroboam as Israel, while Judah stays with David's family.

events.t: Elijah and the prophets of Baal
events.sum: Elijah confronts King Ahab and the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel.

events.t: Isaiah and the prophets of the 700s BC
events.sum: Prophets warn Israel and Judah to return to God and point ahead to a coming king.
Assyria conquers the northern kingdom and scatters its people.
King Hezekiah prays when Assyria surrounds Jerusalem, and the city is spared.
Workers find the Book of the Law in the Temple, and Josiah leads a reform.
Jeremiah warns that Babylon will judge Judah, and promises a new covenant.
Babylon takes Judah's people into captivity in waves. Daniel and Ezekiel serve and prophesy there.

events.t: Babylon destroys Jerusalem and the Temple
events.sum: After a long siege, Babylon burns Jerusalem and Solomon's Temple.
Daniel stays faithful in the lions' den and in the royal court.

events.t: Cyrus lets the exiles go home
events.sum: Persia's king Cyrus allows the Jews to return and rebuild the Temple.
The returned exiles rebuild the Temple despite opposition.
Esther, a Jewish queen of Persia, stops a plot to destroy the Jews.
Ezra comes to Jerusalem and leads the people back to God's Law.
Nehemiah leads the people to rebuild Jerusalem's walls in 52 days.

events.t: Malachi, the last Old Testament prophet
events.sum: Malachi closes the Old Testament by promising a messenger who will prepare the way for the Lord.

events.t: Alexander the Great and Greek culture
events.sum: Alexander conquers the region and Greek language and culture spread. Jewish scholars later translate the Scriptures into Greek.
The Maccabees fight a Greek ruler who defiled the Temple, and rededicate it. Hanukkah recalls this.
The Roman general Pompey takes Jerusalem. Rome rules the land from now through Jesus' day.
Rome's king over Judea rebuilds the Temple on a grand scale and orders the killing of the boys of Bethlehem.

events.t: An angel promises John the Baptist's birth
events.sum: The priest Zechariah is serving in the temple when Gabriel tells him that his aged wife Elizabeth will bear the forerunner of the Lord.

events.t: The angel Gabriel appears to Mary
events.sum: Mary, engaged to Joseph, is told she will conceive and bear the Son of the Most High, and she answers, “Let it be to me according to your word.”
Mary travels south to Elizabeth, whose baby leaps at her greeting, and Mary answers with the song traditionally called the Magnificat.
Elizabeth's son is born and named John, and Zechariah, able to speak again, prophesies about his son and the coming salvation.
Because of a Roman census Joseph and Mary go to David's town, where Jesus is born and laid in a manger.
Angels announce to shepherds in the fields that a Savior has been born, and the shepherds go and find the baby.
Eastern wise men follow a star, ask Herod in Jerusalem where the king of the Jews is to be born, and worship the child with gifts.
Mary and Joseph bring the baby to the temple, where Simeon and Anna recognize him as the promised salvation.
Warned in a dream, Joseph takes Mary and Jesus to Egypt to escape Herod.

events.t: Herod kills the boys of Bethlehem
events.sum: Herod, tricked by the Magi, orders the boys of Bethlehem killed, which Matthew links to Jeremiah's mourning at Ramah.
After Herod's death the family returns from Egypt and makes its home in Galilee, in Nazareth.

events.t: The boy Jesus in the Temple
events.sum: At twelve, Jesus stays behind in the temple, and his parents find him listening to the teachers and asking questions.

events.t: John the Baptist preaches in the wilderness
events.sum: John calls Israel to repent and be baptized, and says that someone far greater is coming after him.
Jesus is baptized by John, the Spirit descends like a dove, and the Father's voice calls him his beloved Son.

events.t: Jesus is tempted in the wilderness
events.sum: After forty days of fasting, Jesus resists the devil's three temptations by quoting Scripture.
Andrew, another disciple, Peter, Philip and Nathanael begin following Jesus after John points him out as the Lamb of God.
At a village wedding Jesus turns water into wine, the first of the signs John records.
Jesus drives out the money changers and sellers and speaks of raising up the temple of his body in three days.
A Pharisee and member of the council comes by night, and Jesus tells him he must be born again and that God so loved the world.
Jesus' disciples baptize in Judea while John baptizes at Aenon, and John says of Jesus, “He must increase, but I must decrease.”
Jesus asks a Samaritan woman for water and offers her living water, and many in the town come to believe.
A royal official begs Jesus to heal his dying son at Capernaum, and Jesus says, “Go; your son will live,” from Cana.
Hearing that John has been arrested, Jesus goes to Galilee and makes Capernaum his base, preaching that the kingdom is near.
In his hometown synagogue Jesus reads Isaiah and says it is fulfilled today, but the people turn against him.
Jesus calls Simon, Andrew, James and John to leave their nets and follow him, and Luke places this after a huge catch of fish.
Jesus teaches with authority and drives an unclean spirit out of a man in the synagogue.

events.t: Peter's mother-in-law and the evening healings
events.sum: Jesus heals Peter's mother-in-law, and that evening the whole town gathers at the door for healing.
Jesus travels through the towns of Galilee teaching, preaching and healing, and large crowds follow him.
A man with leprosy kneels and asks to be made clean, and Jesus touches him and heals him.

events.t: The paralytic lowered through the roof
events.sum: Four friends lower a paralyzed man through the roof, and Jesus forgives his sins and heals him.

events.t: Jesus calls Matthew and eats with sinners
events.sum: Jesus calls the tax collector Levi (Matthew) and dines with tax collectors and sinners, saying he came for the sick.

events.t: Healing at the pool of Bethesda
events.sum: On a Sabbath Jesus heals a man who had been ill for thirty-eight years, then explains his relationship to the Father.

events.t: Lord of the Sabbath in the grainfields
events.sum: When the disciples pick grain on the Sabbath, Jesus calls himself Lord of the Sabbath.

events.t: The man with the withered hand
events.sum: Jesus heals a man's withered hand on the Sabbath in a synagogue, and his opponents begin to plot against him.
After a night in prayer, Jesus names twelve disciples as apostles.
Jesus teaches the Beatitudes, the Lord's Prayer and much more; Luke's parallel is set on a level place.
A Roman centurion asks Jesus to heal his servant without coming to his house, and Jesus marvels at his faith.
At the gate of Nain Jesus stops a funeral and tells a widow's dead son to rise.
After a healing, Jesus' critics say he casts out demons by the prince of demons, and he answers that a divided kingdom cannot stand.
When his mother and brothers come for him, Jesus says that those who do God's will are his family.
From a boat Jesus teaches the crowds in parables, including the sower, the weeds, the mustard seed and the yeast.
A violent squall hits the boat, and Jesus calms the wind and waves with a word.
Jesus frees a man from a legion of demons, who enter a herd of pigs that rushes into the lake.

events.t: Jairus' daughter and the woman with bleeding
events.sum: On the way to Jairus' house a woman is healed by touching Jesus' cloak, and Jesus then raises Jairus' daughter.

events.t: Woes on Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum
events.sum: Jesus warns the towns where most of his miracles were done that they will face judgment if they do not repent.
Jesus sends the Twelve in pairs to preach and heal, with instructions about what to carry and how to respond to rejection.

events.t: John the Baptist is imprisoned and killed
events.sum: Herod Antipas imprisons John for rebuking his marriage, and John is beheaded at Herodias' request.
With five loaves and two fish Jesus feeds a crowd of about five thousand men, the only miracle recorded in all four Gospels.
Jesus comes to the disciples across the stormy lake, and Peter briefly walks toward him.
People bring the sick to touch the edge of Jesus' cloak, and all who touch him are healed.
The crowd finds Jesus at Capernaum, and he says he is the bread of life; many disciples turn back at this teaching.
Pharisees ask why the disciples ignore tradition, and Jesus says what defiles a person comes from the heart.
Jesus enters Gentile territory, and a woman's persistent faith leads him to heal her daughter.

events.t: Healing the deaf man in the Decapolis
events.sum: Jesus heals a deaf man who could hardly speak, and many other sick people, in Gentile country.
A second large crowd is fed with seven loaves and a few fish.
Jesus lands at Magadan (Magdala or Dalmanutha) and refuses the Pharisees' request for a sign.

events.t: A blind man healed at Bethsaida
events.sum: Jesus heals a blind man in two stages, in a story only Mark records.
Peter says Jesus is the Christ, and Jesus begins to speak of his coming suffering.
On a high mountain Jesus shines with glory and speaks with Moses and Elijah, and the Father calls him his Son.

events.t: Jesus heals a boy with a spirit
events.sum: Jesus casts out a spirit that the disciples could not, saying some kinds need prayer.

events.t: The temple tax and the coin in the fish
events.sum: Asked about the temple tax, Jesus sends Peter to catch a fish with a coin in its mouth.
The disciples argue about who is greatest, and Jesus teaches humility, care for little ones and forgiveness.

events.t: Jesus teaches at the Feast of Tabernacles
events.sum: At the autumn feast Jesus teaches in the temple, invites the thirsty to come to him, and sends away the accusers of a woman caught in adultery.

events.t: “I am the light of the world”
events.sum: Jesus says he is the light of the world and that before Abraham was, he is.
Jesus sends a blind man to wash at Siloam and he sees, which leads to a sharp dispute with the Pharisees.
Jesus says he is the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep.
Setting his face toward Jerusalem, Jesus is turned away by a Samaritan village, and he rebukes James and John for wanting to call down fire.
Jesus sends seventy-two ahead of him in pairs, and they return with joy.
Asked who his neighbor is, Jesus tells of a Samaritan who helps a man beaten on the road from Jerusalem to Jericho.
Martha is busy serving while Mary sits at Jesus' feet, and Jesus says Mary has chosen the better part.
At the winter feast Jesus says he and the Father are one, and the crowd tries to stone him.
Jesus weeps and then calls Lazarus out of the tomb after four days.
After Lazarus is raised, the chief priests and Caiaphas decide Jesus must die.
Because of the plot, Jesus leaves public view and stays with his disciples in a town called Ephraim.
Ten men with leprosy are healed, and only one, a Samaritan, comes back to thank Jesus.
Pharisees test Jesus about divorce, and he points back to God's design in creation.
Jesus welcomes children and says the kingdom belongs to such as these.
A rich man asks how to inherit eternal life and goes away sad when Jesus tells him to sell all.
Jesus tells the Twelve for the third time that he will be killed and rise, and he teaches that greatness is serving.
As Jesus leaves Jericho a blind beggar cries out to him and receives his sight.
Jesus invites himself to the house of the chief tax collector Zacchaeus, who gives half his goods to the poor.
A woman pours expensive perfume on Jesus shortly before his death, and he says she has prepared him for burial.
Riding a donkey, Jesus enters Jerusalem to cries of “Hosanna” from the crowds.
Jesus curses a fruitless fig tree, and the next day it has withered; he uses this to teach about faith.
Jesus overturns the money changers' tables, saying the temple should be a house of prayer.

events.t: Questions and teaching in the Temple
events.sum: Leaders challenge Jesus' authority, and he answers about taxes, the resurrection and the greatest commandment.

events.t: Some Greeks ask to see Jesus
events.sum: Greeks come to Philip wanting to see Jesus, and he speaks of the grain of wheat that must die and of being lifted up.

events.t: Woes on the scribes and Pharisees
events.sum: Jesus sharply warns against the religious leaders' hypocrisy and laments over Jerusalem.
Jesus watches the crowd give and says a poor widow gave more than all the rest.
On the Mount of Olives Jesus speaks of the temple's fall, coming trials and his return, and tells parables about being ready.
Judas goes to the chief priests and agrees to hand Jesus over for thirty pieces of silver.
At the Passover meal Jesus washes his disciples' feet, gives them the bread and cup, and says one of them will betray him.
Jesus comforts his disciples, promises the Spirit and says he is the vine and they are the branches.
Jesus prays for himself, his disciples and all who will believe through them.
Jesus prays in agony in the garden, asking that the cup pass but submitting to the Father's will.
Judas leads a crowd with swords and clubs to arrest Jesus, and the disciples flee.

events.t: Jesus before the high priest; Peter denies him
events.sum: Jesus is questioned by Annas and Caiaphas while Peter denies knowing him three times.
Judas, seeing Jesus condemned, returns the silver and takes his own life, and the priests buy a field with the money.
Pilate questions Jesus, finds no guilt, and finally gives him up to be crucified.
Pilate sends Jesus to Herod, who mocks him and sends him back.
Soldiers mock Jesus, and Simon of Cyrene is made to carry his cross.
Jesus is crucified between two criminals, forgives those who killed him, and dies.
Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus lay Jesus in a new tomb, and a guard is set.
Women find the tomb empty, and Mary Magdalene meets the risen Jesus.
The risen Jesus walks with two disciples and is recognized when he breaks bread.

events.t: Jesus appears in the upper room
events.sum: Jesus appears to the gathered disciples, shows them his hands and side, and opens the Scriptures to them.
A week later Jesus appears to Thomas, who says, “My Lord and my God!”
The risen Jesus cooks breakfast for seven disciples on the shore and restores Peter.
Jesus meets the eleven on a mountain and sends them to make disciples of all nations.
Jesus blesses the disciples and is taken up into heaven.

events.t: Jesus’ last words and the promise of the Spirit
events.sum: For forty days the risen Jesus teaches the apostles about the kingdom, tells them to wait in Jerusalem for the Holy Spirit, and is taken up into a cloud. Two angels say he will return the same way.

events.t: The believers pray and choose Matthias
events.sum: About 120 believers wait and pray together. Peter reads Judas's fall in the Psalms, and the lot falls to Matthias to join the Eleven.
The Holy Spirit comes on Jesus' followers in Jerusalem, Peter preaches, and about three thousand believe.
Acts lists "visitors from Rome," both Jews and converts to Judaism, among the crowd at Pentecost. Some may have carried the gospel home, and a church existed in Rome long before Paul came.
events.n: Romans does not say who founded the church in Rome. Paul writes to a church he has not visited (Romans 1:10-15).

events.t: Peter preaches and three thousand are baptized
events.sum: Peter says the crucified Jesus is both Lord and Messiah, quotes Joel and David, and calls the crowd to repent. About three thousand are baptized that day.

events.t: The first church shares life together
events.sum: The new believers learn from the apostles, break bread in homes, pray, and share their goods with anyone in need.
The apostles heal, preach and are arrested, and believers share what they have.

events.t: A lame man healed at the Beautiful Gate
events.sum: Peter and John, going up to the three o'clock prayer, tell a man lame from birth to walk in the name of Jesus. He enters the temple leaping and praising God.
A crowd gathers. Peter says God has glorified the Servant they handed over, and calls them to repent so that times of refreshing may come.

events.t: Peter and John before the council
events.sum: Arrested by the temple guard, the two are questioned by Annas, Caiaphas and the council. Peter answers that there is salvation in no one else. They are warned and released.
The believers pray for boldness, the place shakes, and they are filled again. Barnabas sells a field and lays the money at the apostles' feet.
A couple sell property and keep back part of the price while claiming to give all of it. Peter exposes the lie, and both die. Great fear falls on the church.

events.t: The apostles arrested and freed by an angel
events.sum: Many are healed in the shadow of Peter. The high priest jails the apostles, but an angel opens the doors at night and sends them back to teach in the temple.
The apostles say they must obey God rather than men. The Pharisee Gamaliel urges caution: if this is of God, no one can stop it. They are flogged and released, rejoicing.
Greek-speaking widows are overlooked in the daily food. The apostles ask the church to choose seven, including Stephen and Philip, and the word of God spreads.
Stephen is accused of speaking against the temple and the law. He retells Israel's story from Abraham to Solomon and says the Righteous One has now been betrayed and murdered.
Stephen, the first Christian martyr, is stoned. Saul looks on.

Scattered by persecution, Philip preaches in a Samaritan city. Many believe and are baptized. Peter and John come down, and the Spirit is given. Simon the sorcerer offers money for the power and is rebuked.
Philip meets an Ethiopian official reading Isaiah 53 and explains that it points to Jesus. The official believes and is baptized.

events.t: Saul meets Jesus on the Damascus road
events.sum: The persecutor Saul meets the risen Jesus, is blinded, and becomes Paul, the apostle to the nations.
The Lord sends a frightened disciple named Ananias to Saul, who is praying at Judas's house on Straight Street. Ananias lays hands on him; scales fall from his eyes, and he is baptized.

events.t: Paul goes to Arabia and returns to Damascus
events.sum: Paul says that after God revealed His Son to him he did not consult anyone or go up to Jerusalem, but "went into Arabia and later returned to Damascus."
events.n: Acts does not mention Arabia. The Nabataean kingdom is probably meant, and the letter gives no reason for the trip.

events.t: Saul preaches and escapes in a basket
events.sum: Saul proclaims in the synagogues that Jesus is the Son of God. When a plot forms to kill him, friends lower him in a basket through an opening in the wall at night.
The disciples fear Saul until Barnabas brings him to the apostles and tells how he met the Lord. Saul speaks boldly, then is sent home to Tarsus when Greek-speaking Jews seek to kill him.

events.t: Fifteen days with Cephas in Jerusalem
events.sum: After three years Paul goes up to Jerusalem "to confer with Cephas" and stays fifteen days. He sees no other apostle "except James, the Lord's brother."
events.n: Acts 9:26-30 tells the same visit, with Barnabas bringing Saul to the apostles.

events.sum: The quiet years. Saul goes to Tarsus and Syria and Cilicia. Barnabas later comes looking for him.

events.t: Paul in Syria and Cilicia, unknown to the churches of Judea
events.sum: Paul goes to Syria and Cilicia. The churches of Judea know him only by report: "The man who formerly persecuted us is now preaching the faith he once tried to destroy."
Peter finds a man named Aeneas who had been bedridden eight years. 'Jesus Christ heals you,' he says, and Aeneas gets up. Many in Lydda and Sharon turn to the Lord.
A disciple named Tabitha (Dorcas), known for her kindness, dies. Peter kneels, prays, and says 'Tabitha, arise.' She opens her eyes, and Peter stays in Joppa with Simon the tanner.
A Roman centurion who fears God and prays and gives alms sees an angel in a vision. He is told to send for Simon Peter at Joppa.
On the roof at noon Peter sees a sheet of animals let down from heaven and hears, 'What God has made clean, do not call common.' Three men from Cornelius arrive at the door.
Peter preaches to the Roman centurion Cornelius, and the Spirit falls on Gentiles.

events.t: Peter explains to the church in Jerusalem
events.sum: Believers criticize Peter for eating with uncircumcised men. He tells the whole story, and the church says, 'Then to the Gentiles also God has granted repentance that leads to life.'
In Antioch, a mixed church of Jews and Gentiles is first called Christian.

events.t: Relief for Judea and Herod's persecution
events.sum: A prophet named Agabus foretells a famine, and Barnabas and Saul carry a gift to Judea. Herod Agrippa I kills James the brother of John and jails Peter, but an angel frees him and he goes to Mark's mother's house.
Herod accepts a crowd's cry that he speaks like a god, and an angel of the Lord strikes him down. The word of God grows and multiplies.

events.t: Paul takes the gospel to the nations
events.sum: Paul plants churches across the Roman world on three journeys and is taken to Rome.
Paul and Barnabas take the gospel to Cyprus and what is now Turkey.
events.n: Acts gives no calendar dates. These years follow the common reading of Paul's life, with Gallio at Corinth about AD 51-52 as the anchor.

events.sum: While the prophets and teachers worship and fast, the Holy Spirit says, 'Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul.' The church lays hands on them and sends them off. This is the start of the first missionary journey.
From Seleucia the team sails to Cyprus, Barnabas's home island. At Salamis they preach in the synagogues, with John Mark as their helper.
The proconsul Sergius Paulus asks to hear the word of God. A sorcerer named Elymas opposes them and is struck blind. The proconsul believes. From here Luke calls him Paul.
The team sails to Perga on the south coast of Asia Minor. John Mark leaves them and returns to Jerusalem. Paul later refuses to take him on the second journey.

In the synagogue Paul retells Israel's story to David and declares that through Jesus forgiveness is proclaimed. The next Sabbath the crowds come, many Jews contradict, and Paul turns to the Gentiles. They are driven out.
Paul and Barnabas speak so that a great number of Jews and Greeks believe. The city splits, and when a plot to stone them forms, they leave for Lystra and Derbe.

events.t: Lystra: the crowd calls them gods
events.sum: Paul heals a man who has never walked. The crowd calls Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes and tries to offer sacrifices. Paul tells them to turn from these vain things to the living God.
Jews from Antioch and Iconium win over the crowd, and Paul is stoned and dragged out of the city as dead. The disciples gather around him; he gets up and goes back in.
The next day Paul and Barnabas go to Derbe, make many disciples, then retrace their steps and appoint elders in every church with prayer and fasting.
Paul and Barnabas sail from Attalia, gather the church, and tell how God 'had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles.' They stay a long time.

events.t: Paul meets the leaders in Jerusalem, with Titus
events.sum: Fourteen years later Paul goes up with Barnabas and Titus and sets his gospel before the leaders. Titus is not made to be circumcised, and James, Cephas and John give Paul and Barnabas "the right hand of fellowship."
events.n: Scholars disagree whether this is the visit of Acts 11:30, a private meeting held at the time of the Council of Acts 15, or a different visit. The timeline places it just before the Council.

events.sum: Church leaders agree Gentiles are saved by grace, not by keeping the Law of Moses.
Peter stops eating with Gentile believers when men come from James, and others follow, even Barnabas. Paul opposes him "to his face" because "he stood to be condemned."
events.n: Acts does not tell this. It probably came after the Council, but Paul does not say when, and some scholars place it before.

events.t: Paul writes to the churches of Galatia
events.sum: Paul writes a sharp letter: the Galatians are turning to "a different gospel," and he says people are made right with God by faith in Christ, not by works of the law. He ends with large letters in his own hand.
events.n: The date depends on where the churches were. The south Galatian view (the churches of Acts 13-14) allows an early date, about AD 48-49, before the Council. The north Galatian view and some others give a later date, during the third journey (about AD 53-56). The letter does not name the place where it was written.

events.sum: The Roman historian Suetonius says Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome after constant disturbances instigated by "Chrestus." Priscilla and Aquila leave Rome and meet Paul in Corinth.
events.n: The year AD 49 comes from the later writer Orosius, and some scholars prefer AD 41. Jewish believers could return after Claudius died in AD 54.

events.sum: James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, writes to the twelve tribes in the Dispersion: short, direct teaching on trials, wisdom, riches, the tongue, prayer and a faith that acts.
events.n: The letter does not date itself. The traditional author, James the brother of Jesus and leader of the Jerusalem church, was killed about AD 62 according to Josephus, so on that view it is earlier. It never mentions the Gentile question of Acts 15, which some take as a sign that it is very early, and others as a sign that it comes from a Jewish Christian setting that never faced it. Other scholars date it later, and some think it was written in James's name after his death. The first writer to cite it by name as Scripture is Origen, in the early 3rd century; Eusebius says some doubted it, though it was read in most churches.

events.t: Joy in trials, wisdom, and the crown of life
events.sum: The testing of faith produces perseverance; anyone who lacks wisdom may ask God; God tempts no one, and every good gift is from above.

events.t: Doers of the word and pure religion
events.sum: Be quick to listen, slow to speak; do not only hear the word but do it; pure religion is to care for orphans and widows and keep oneself unstained from the world.
Do not honor the rich man in fine clothes over the poor man in shabby clothes; God has chosen the poor to be rich in faith, and mercy triumphs over judgment.
Faith that does nothing for a hungry brother is dead; Abraham and Rahab show faith at work.
events.n: Paul says a person is justified by faith and not by works of the law (Galatians 2:16); James says a person is justified by deeds and not by faith alone (2:24). Many readers think they use "works" and "faith" in different senses and address different problems; others see a real tension, and the question has been argued since at least the Reformation.

events.sum: A bit, a rudder and a spark show how a small thing steers a large one; no one can tame the tongue, and blessing and cursing should not come from the same mouth.

events.t: Passions at war: submit to God
events.sum: Quarrels come from desires at war within; friendship with the world is hostility toward God; submit to God, resist the devil, and humble yourselves.
Wealth that rots, and wages held back from the field workers, cry out to the Lord of Hosts.
Like the farmer who waits for the rains, the readers are to be patient; the prophets and Job are examples; let your yes be yes.

events.t: The prayer of faith and Elijah
events.sum: The sick are to call the elders to pray and anoint with oil; confess sins to each other; Elijah prayed and it did not rain for three and a half years; bring back the one who wanders.
Paul takes the gospel to Macedonia and Greece, including Philippi, Athens and Corinth.
A sharp dispute over taking John Mark ends their partnership. Barnabas takes Mark to Cyprus; Paul chooses Silas and heads through Syria and Cilicia. This begins the second journey.
Paul finds a disciple named Timothy, son of a Jewish mother and Greek father, well spoken of. Paul has him circumcised and takes him along.

events.t: The vision of the man of Macedonia
events.sum: Forbidden by the Spirit to speak in Asia or Bithynia, Paul reaches Troas. In a night vision a man of Macedonia pleads, 'Come over to Macedonia and help us.' The narrative changes to 'we' here.
By the river on the Sabbath, Paul speaks to a group of women. Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth, opens her heart, and she and her household are baptized.

Paul frees a slave girl from a spirit. Her owners drag Paul and Silas before the magistrates, who have them beaten and jailed. At midnight an earthquake opens the doors, and the jailer asks, 'What must I do to be saved?'
For three Sabbaths Paul argues from Scripture that the Messiah had to suffer and rise. A mob accuses the believers of saying there is another king, Jesus.
The Bereans receive the word eagerly and examine the Scriptures daily to see if these things are so. When agitators come from Thessalonica, Paul is sent to the coast.

events.t: Paul at the Areopagus in Athens
events.sum: Distressed by the idols, Paul speaks in the marketplace and then to the Areopagus council. He points to an altar 'to the unknown god,' quotes Greek poets, and says God will judge the world by the man he raised from the dead.

Paul works with Aquila and Priscilla, tent-makers, and teaches in the synagogue. When opposition rises he moves next door. The Lord says in a night vision, 'I have many in this city who are my people.' Gallio dismisses the charge against him.

Timothy comes back with good news about the young church in Thessalonica, and Paul writes to thank them, to answer their questions and to comfort them about those who have died. This may be the earliest letter of Paul that survives.
events.n: The letter does not name its place of writing. Corinth fits Acts 18:5, where Silas and Timothy rejoin Paul. Galatians may be earlier if it was written before the Council (AD 48-49).

events.t: Paul, alone in Athens, sends Timothy to Thessalonica
events.sum: Paul could "bear it no longer" and sent Timothy to strengthen the church and find out if they had held firm. Timothy came back to him with good news.

events.t: The hope for "those who sleep in death"
events.sum: Paul tells the believers not to grieve "like the rest, who are without hope," since the dead in Christ will rise first and all will be with the Lord.

events.d: c. AD 50-52 (soon after the first letter)
events.sum: Silvanus and Timothy are still with Paul as he writes again to a church under pressure. He promises relief when the Lord is revealed, corrects a false report that the day has come, and tells the idle to work.
events.n: Some scholars doubt that Paul wrote 2 Thessalonians, and others hold that he did. Those who accept it usually date it a few months after the first letter.

events.t: A report that "the Day of the Lord has already come"
events.sum: Someone says the Day has already come, by a "spirit or message or letter seeming to be from us." Paul answers that "the rebellion" and "the man of lawlessness" must come first, and that something is now restraining him.
events.n: This is one of the hardest passages in the New Testament, and readers differ on what it describes.

events.t: "If anyone is unwilling to work, he shall not eat"
events.sum: Some in the church had stopped working and were "busybodies." Paul points to his own example of working "night and day" and tells them to "begin working quietly to earn their own living."

events.t: A vow at Cenchreae; a short stop at Ephesus
events.sum: Paul cuts his hair at Cenchreae because of a vow, sails to Ephesus where he reasons in the synagogue, leaves Priscilla and Aquila there, and returns by Caesarea and Jerusalem to Antioch.
Paul spends about three years in Ephesus and then revisits the churches.
Apollos, a learned Jew from Alexandria, preaches fervently but knows only the baptism of John. Priscilla and Aquila take him aside and explain the way of God more accurately.

events.t: Paul in Ephesus: the Spirit, Tyrannus, the burning scrolls
events.sum: Paul finds twelve disciples who know only John's baptism and baptizes them in Jesus' name. For two years he teaches in the hall of Tyrannus. Handkerchiefs, exorcists and burned magic scrolls worth fifty thousand silver pieces mark the time.
Claudius dies in October AD 54 and Nero, then sixteen, becomes emperor. Jews, including Priscilla and Aquila, are free to return to Rome, and Paul greets them there in Romans 16.
Paul writes "I wrote you in my letter not to associate with sexually immoral people." That earlier letter has not survived, and the Corinthians misunderstood it.
events.n: What we call 1 Corinthians is at least the second letter. 2 Corinthians 2:3-4 and 7:8 may refer to yet another painful letter.

events.t: News from Chloe's household and a letter from Corinth
events.sum: Some of Chloe's household tell Paul of quarrels in the church, and the Corinthians send questions in writing. Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus arrive in Ephesus.
Paul answers the quarrels, the scandal, the lawsuits, marriage, idol food, the Lord's Supper, spiritual gifts and the resurrection. He plans to stay in Ephesus until Pentecost.
events.n: Most scholars date the letter to the last year or two of Paul's time in Ephesus, between about AD 53 and 55.

events.t: The oldest creed: Christ died and was raised
events.sum: Paul passes on what he received "as of first importance": Christ's death for our sins, his burial, his resurrection on the third day, and his appearances to Cephas, the Twelve, more than five hundred, James and Paul himself.
events.n: Most scholars think this wording goes back to within a few years of the crucifixion, long before any Gospel was written.

events.t: Timothy and Erastus are sent ahead
events.sum: Paul sends Timothy through Macedonia toward Corinth, and plans to follow after Pentecost. Timothy may arrive before the letter does.
Demetrius, a silversmith who makes shrines of Artemis, rouses the city. The crowd chants 'Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!' for two hours until the town clerk calms them.

events.t: Paul despairs of life in Asia
events.sum: Paul says he and his coworkers "despaired even of life" in the province of Asia and felt "under the sentence of death." The letter does not say what happened.
events.n: Some link it to the riot at Ephesus in Acts 19, but the letter gives no details.

events.sum: Paul makes a short second visit to Corinth that goes badly and ends in hurt on both sides. Acts does not mention it.
events.n: Most scholars place this visit between 1 Corinthians and 2 Corinthians. It makes the visit in Acts 20:2-3 Paul's third.

events.sum: Paul writes a severe letter "out of great distress and anguish of heart" and sends it to Corinth. He first regrets it, then rejoices that it led the church to repentance.
events.n: This letter is lost, or it survives as part of 2 Corinthians 10-13, or it is 1 Corinthians. Scholars have argued all three.

events.sum: Paul finds "a door stood open" at Troas but has "no peace in my spirit" because Titus is not there with news from Corinth, so he goes on to Macedonia.
Titus arrives with news that the Corinthians have repented and grieve with Paul, and Paul is comforted.
Paul writes to Corinth about comfort in suffering, the ministry of the new covenant, reconciliation, the collection, and his authority. He plans to come with Macedonians.
events.n: Many scholars think chapters 10-13 were a separate letter, written before or after chapters 1-9, joined later.

events.t: The collection for Jerusalem is finished
events.sum: Paul urges Corinth to complete the gift they began "last year," sends Titus and two other brothers ahead, and says God "loves a cheerful giver."
Paul spends three months in Greece. He warns that he is ready to come "a third time," and Romans is written from Corinth during these months.

events.t: Paul writes the letter to the Romans
events.sum: During his three months in Greece Paul writes to the church in Rome from Corinth. Tertius writes it down, and Gaius, Erastus and others send greetings.
events.n: Scholars place the letter between about AD 55 and 58. Corinth fits the clues in Romans 16 best.

events.sum: Paul commends Phoebe, a servant of the church at Cenchreae, and asks the Romans to receive her and help her. She is probably the one who brought the letter to Rome.
Macedonia and Achaia have given to the poor among the believers in Jerusalem. Paul is about to carry the gift there and asks the Romans to pray for him.
Paul has finished his work in the East. He hopes to see Rome on his way to Spain, but he must go to Jerusalem first.
events.n: The New Testament does not say whether Paul reached Spain.

events.sum: After travelling through Macedonia and Greece, Paul meets the church at Troas on the first day of the week. A young man named Eutychus falls from a window during his long talk, and Paul raises him.
Paul summons the elders from Ephesus and tells them he is going to Jerusalem bound in the Spirit. 'It is more blessed to give than to receive.' They weep, embrace him, and walk him to the ship.
Sailing by Cos, Rhodes and Patara, Paul reaches Tyre. The disciples there warn him through the Spirit not to go on to Jerusalem. The families kneel with him on the beach and pray.

Paul stays with Philip the evangelist and his four prophesying daughters. Agabus binds his own hands with Paul's belt and says the Jews will bind the owner of the belt. Paul says he is ready to die for the Lord.

events.t: Paul is arrested at the temple
events.sum: Jews from Asia accuse Paul of bringing Greeks into the temple and drag him out. Roman soldiers rescue him from the mob and arrest him.
events.n: Paul's dates are approximate. Scholars place his arrest between about AD 55 and 58.

events.t: The Temple wall that kept Gentiles out
events.sum: Paul is seized after a rumor that he took a Gentile past the Temple barrier. Later he writes that Christ "has torn down the dividing wall of hostility" and made Jew and Gentile "one new man."
events.n: Many scholars think Paul has the Temple barrier in mind in Ephesians 2:14, and others read the wall as the law. Paul does not say.

events.sum: From the barracks steps Paul addresses the crowd in Aramaic and tells his story. At the word 'Gentiles' they erupt. The tribune orders him examined by flogging until Paul says he is a Roman citizen.

Paul splits the council by saying he is on trial for the resurrection of the dead; Pharisees and Sadducees quarrel. That night the Lord says, 'Take courage, for as you have testified about me in Jerusalem, so you must testify also in Rome.'

events.t: The plot and the night ride
events.sum: Forty men vow not to eat until they kill Paul. His nephew hears and tells the tribune, who sends Paul with 470 soldiers by night to the governor Felix at Caesarea.

The high priest's lawyer Tertullus accuses Paul. Paul replies that he came to worship, not to stir riots, and that the real issue is the resurrection. Felix keeps him in custody for two years, hoping for a bribe.
The new governor Festus asks if Paul will be tried at Jerusalem. Paul, knowing the danger, says 'I appeal to Caesar.' Festus replies, 'To Caesar you shall go.'

King Agrippa II and his sister Bernice come to hear him. Paul tells of his Damascus road meeting and his commission, and asks Agrippa, 'Do you believe the prophets?' The king says Paul could have been set free had he not appealed to Caesar.
Paul, other prisoners, Luke and Aristarchus sail under the centurion Julius. At Myra they change to an Alexandrian grain ship and slowly reach Fair Havens on Crete.

Against Paul's advice the ship leaves for a better harbor. A northeaster seizes it and drives it for fourteen days. An angel tells Paul that all 276 aboard will be saved, and Paul encourages them to eat.

The ship runs aground on a sandbar and breaks up. All reach shore. A viper bites Paul's hand and he shakes it into the fire; the islanders call him a god. He heals the father of Publius and many others.

After three months they sail in another Alexandrian ship, landing at Puteoli. Believers there host Paul for a week, and brothers from Rome meet him on the Appian Way. Paul thanks God and takes courage.
Paul calls the Jewish leaders together, then for two years in his own rented house welcomes all who come, proclaiming the kingdom of God with all boldness and without hindrance.
events.n: Acts ends here without telling the outcome of his appeal to Caesar.

events.t: Paul writes to the Ephesians from prison
events.sum: Paul, "the prisoner of Christ Jesus for the sake of you Gentiles," writes of God's plan to unite all things in Christ, the one new people of Jews and Gentiles, and how to live as the church, ending with the armor of God.
events.n: The usual view is Rome, with Colossians and Philemon. Caesarea (about AD 57-59) is also suggested, and some scholars think a follower of Paul wrote Ephesians after his death. The letter does not name the place.

events.sum: Tychicus, "the beloved brother and faithful servant in the Lord," is sent to the churches of Asia to tell them about Paul and encourage their hearts. He also carries Colossians and goes with Onesimus.

events.t: A letter for the churches of Asia?
events.sum: The oldest manuscripts leave out "in Ephesus" in 1:1, and Paul tells the Colossians to read "the letter from Laodicea." Some scholars think Ephesians was a circular letter sent to several churches in Asia.
events.n: This is a theory. Early copies and Marcion's collection give different readings, and nobody knows for sure.

events.t: Paul writes to the Philippians from prison
events.sum: Paul and Timothy write to the church at Philippi. Paul is in chains, the whole palace guard knows why, and he thanks the church for its gift. The letter is full of joy: "Rejoice in the Lord always."
events.n: Rome is the usual view, with Ephesians, Colossians and Philemon. Ephesus (about AD 53-55) and Caesarea (about AD 57-59) have also been suggested, because the letter implies several trips between Paul and Philippi. Nobody knows in what order the prison letters were written.

events.t: Epaphroditus brings the gift and almost dies
events.sum: The church at Philippi sends a gift by Epaphroditus. He falls so ill that he is "nearly unto death," recovers, and is sent home with the letter.

events.d: c. AD 60-62 (the hymn may be older)
events.sum: Christ, "existing in the form of God," empties Himself, takes the form of a servant, and dies on a cross. God then gives Him "the name above all names," and every tongue will confess that Jesus Christ is Lord.
events.n: Many scholars think Paul quotes an earlier hymn. Others think he wrote it for this letter. Either way, it is among the earliest written statements about Christ.

events.t: Timothy is to be sent to Philippi
events.sum: Paul hopes to send Timothy soon, once he sees how his own case goes, and trusts that he himself will come.

events.t: Paul writes to the Colossians from prison
events.sum: Paul and Timothy write to a church Paul has never visited, after Epaphras brings news from the Lycus Valley. They warn against teaching that adds rules and visions to Christ, and say that in Him "all the fullness of the Deity dwells in bodily form."
events.n: Rome is the usual view, with Ephesians, Philippians and Philemon. Ephesus and Caesarea have also been suggested. Some scholars think a follower of Paul wrote Colossians, and others hold that Paul wrote it. Nobody knows in what order the prison letters were written.

events.t: The Son is the image of the invisible God
events.d: c. AD 60-62 (the hymn may be older)
events.sum: Christ is the image of the invisible God and the firstborn over all creation. All things were created through Him and for Him, and through Him God reconciles all things, "by making peace through the blood of His cross."
events.n: Many scholars think Paul quotes or shapes an early hymn. Others think he wrote the passage for this letter.

events.t: Epaphras brings news and prays for the valley
events.sum: Epaphras, who is from Colossae, founded or taught the church there. He tells Paul of their love, and Paul says he "is always wrestling in prayer" for the churches of Colossae, Laodicea and Hierapolis.

events.t: A warning against philosophy and rules
events.sum: Paul warns that no one should take them "captive through philosophy and empty deception," or judge them by food, festivals or the worship of angels. These are "a shadow of the things to come, but the body that casts it belongs to Christ."
events.n: The letter does not name the teachers, and scholars still debate who they were.

events.t: Tychicus and Onesimus carry the letter
events.sum: Tychicus delivers the letter and gives the news about Paul. Onesimus, who is "one of you," goes with him, and he is almost certainly the slave for whom Paul writes to Philemon.
Paul, in prison, writes a short personal letter to Philemon, who hosts a church in his house, to ask him to welcome back Onesimus, a slave who has come to faith, as a beloved brother.
events.n: The letter does not say where Paul was held. Rome is the traditional answer, with Ephesus and Caesarea also proposed. It was probably written at about the same time as Colossians, since both name Epaphras, Mark, Aristarchus, Luke and Demas, and Tychicus and Onesimus carried Colossians (Colossians 4:7-9). Almost everyone accepts that Paul wrote Philemon.

events.sum: Paul asks Philemon to receive Onesimus, "no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother."
Paul writes with his own hand that he will repay whatever Onesimus owes, and asks Philemon to receive him as he would receive Paul.

events.t: Paul asks for a guest room
events.sum: Paul hopes, through the prayers of the church, to be restored to them, and asks Philemon to prepare a guest room.

Paul has gone on to Macedonia and left Timothy at Ephesus. He writes to guide him in dealing with false teachers, ordering the church and caring for its people. This is the first of the three "pastoral letters" (1 and 2 Timothy and Titus).
events.n: If Paul wrote it, the letter fits after the end of Acts, when Paul was free to travel again. Acts does not tell this part of his life. Some scholars think the three pastoral letters were written after Paul's death by someone using his name, and others hold that Paul wrote them.

events.t: Timothy is left at Ephesus to face false teachers
events.sum: Paul asks Timothy to "stay on at Ephesus" and to tell certain men not to teach false doctrines or follow "myths and endless genealogies."

events.t: Paul: "Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners"
events.sum: Paul calls himself "the worst of sinners" and says he was shown mercy as an example to those who would believe.

events.t: Overseers, deacons and the household of God
events.sum: Paul lists what to look for in overseers and deacons, mostly matters of character, and calls the church "the household of God," the pillar and foundation of the truth.

events.t: "Guard what has been entrusted to you"
events.sum: Paul ends with a charge to Timothy: pursue godliness, fight the good fight, be generous with wealth, and keep safe the teaching he has received.

Paul writes to Titus, whom he left on Crete to finish the work there. He gives the qualities of elders, warns against rebellious teachers, describes how each group in the church should live, and asks Titus to join him at Nicopolis for the winter.
events.n: If Paul wrote it, the letter fits the years after the end of Acts, near the time of 1 Timothy, and before the last imprisonment of 2 Timothy. Acts does not tell this part of his life or the visit to Crete. The letter does not say where Paul was when he wrote. Some scholars think the three pastoral letters were written after Paul's death by someone using his name.

events.t: Titus is left on Crete to appoint elders
events.sum: Paul says he left Titus in Crete to "set in order what was unfinished and appoint elders in every town."

Paul says the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to everyone, and that it trains believers to live upright lives as they await "the blessed hope and glorious appearance of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ."
Paul says God saved us, "not by the righteous deeds we had done, but according to His mercy, through the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit."

events.t: Paul plans to winter at Nicopolis
events.sum: Paul asks Titus to come to him at Nicopolis as soon as Artemas or Tychicus arrives, "because I have decided to winter there."
Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, writes to the exiles of the Dispersion in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia: a letter of hope for believers living as outsiders and under pressure.
events.n: The letter does not date itself. Tradition says Peter died at Rome under Nero, and Nero's persecution of Christians there began after the fire of AD 64, so on the traditional view the letter was written between about AD 62 and 65. "Babylon" (5:13) is usually taken as Rome. Some scholars think the polished Greek and the lack of personal memories of Jesus point to a later date, after AD 70, with Silvanus or a follower writing in Peter's name; others hold that Silvanus (5:12) shaped the Greek for Peter, and that the letter is his.

events.t: A living hope and an inheritance that cannot fade
events.sum: Born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ, believers have an inheritance kept in heaven, and they are shielded by God's power.

events.t: Proven faith: more precious than gold
events.sum: Trials prove the genuineness of faith as fire proves gold; the readers love and believe in a Lord they have not seen.

events.t: Redeemed with the blood of a lamb
events.sum: Be holy as God is holy; the readers were bought not with silver or gold but with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot.

events.t: The living stone and the cornerstone
events.sum: Christ is the living stone, rejected by men but chosen by God; those who come to him are built up as a spiritual house.

events.t: A chosen people, a royal priesthood
events.sum: The titles of Israel at Sinai are given to the church: a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God's own possession.

events.t: Servants and the example of Christ
events.sum: Slaves are told to bear unjust suffering as Christ did, who left an example and bore our sins in his body on the tree.

events.t: Wives and husbands: a gentle and quiet spirit
events.sum: Wives are to win unbelieving husbands by their conduct; husbands are to honor their wives as fellow heirs of the gracious gift of life.

events.t: "The reason for the hope that is in you"
events.sum: Do not fear what they fear; sanctify Christ as Lord and be ready to give a defense, with gentleness and respect.

events.t: The spirits in prison, Noah and baptism
events.sum: Christ suffered once, was made alive in the Spirit, and preached to the spirits in prison; the ark and the flood are likened to baptism; he is now at God's right hand.
events.n: This is one of the hardest passages in the New Testament. The main readings are that Christ preached through Noah to his generation, that he announced his victory to the rebel angels of Genesis 6 and 1 Enoch, or that he went to the realm of the dead. The letter does not settle it.

events.t: The fiery trial: suffering as a Christian
events.sum: Do not be surprised at the fiery trial; if anyone suffers as a Christian, he should not be ashamed but glorify God in that name.

events.t: Shepherd the flock; the Chief Shepherd
events.sum: Elders are to shepherd the flock willingly, as examples, and will receive the unfading crown of glory when the Chief Shepherd appears.

events.t: The roaring lion and the God of all grace
events.sum: Humble yourselves, cast your anxiety on God, resist the devil who prowls like a roaring lion; after a little suffering the God of all grace will restore you.
Peter closes with greetings from the church in Babylon and from his son Mark, and writes through Silvanus.

Simon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ, writes to believers who share a faith as precious as the apostles': a farewell letter that warns against false teaching and points to Christ's return.
events.n: The letter does not date itself. If Peter wrote it, it comes from his last years, after 1 Peter and before his death, which tradition places at Rome under Nero in the 60s. Many scholars think it was written in his name after his death, some say between about AD 80 and 120. The author, the date and the readers are all debated.

events.t: Everything for life and godliness: partakers of the divine nature
events.sum: God's divine power has given believers everything they need, with precious promises through which they share in the divine nature and escape the corruption of the world.

events.t: Add to your faith: from virtue to love
events.sum: The readers are to add virtue, knowledge, self-control, perseverance, godliness, brotherly kindness and love to their faith, and to make their calling and election sure.

events.t: The tent will soon be laid aside
events.sum: Peter says he will keep reminding them as long as he lives in the tent of his body, because the Lord has shown him that his departure is near.

events.t: Eyewitnesses of His majesty on the holy mountain
events.sum: The apostles did not follow cleverly devised fables: they saw Christ's majesty and heard the voice from heaven on the holy mountain.

events.t: The word of the prophets, carried along by the Holy Spirit
events.sum: The prophetic word is a lamp in a dark place until the day dawns; no prophecy came by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.
As false prophets arose among the people, so false teachers will come among the readers, secretly bringing in destructive heresies and exploiting them out of greed.

events.t: Angels, the flood and Sodom: God knows how to rescue the godly
events.sum: God did not spare angels who sinned, the ancient world in the flood, or Sodom and Gomorrah, but he kept Noah and Lot, and he knows how to hold the unrighteous for the day of judgment.
events.n: Chapter 2 runs close to Jude 4-18, and most scholars think 2 Peter used Jude. The angels in chains of darkness are usually linked to Genesis 6:1-4 and the Book of Enoch.

events.sum: The false teachers have left the straight way and followed Balaam son of Beor, who loved the wages of wickedness and was rebuked by a donkey that spoke.

events.t: The dog returns to its vomit
events.sum: Those who have escaped the world's corruption and are entangled again are worse off than at first; the proverbs of the dog and the washed sow describe them.

events.t: Scoffers: Where is the promise of His coming?
events.sum: Scoffers will say nothing has changed since the fathers died; Peter answers that the world once perished by water and is now kept for fire.

events.t: A day like a thousand years: the Lord is patient
events.sum: With the Lord a day is like a thousand years; he is not slow but patient, not wanting anyone to perish, and the Day of the Lord will come like a thief.

events.t: A new heaven and a new earth
events.sum: Since all this will be dissolved, believers are to live in holiness and godliness, looking for a new heaven and a new earth where righteousness dwells.

events.t: Our beloved brother Paul and the rest of the Scriptures
events.sum: The Lord's patience means salvation, as Paul also wrote; some parts of his letters are hard to understand, and the ignorant and unstable distort them as they do the other Scriptures.

events.t: Grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior
events.sum: Be on guard against the error of the lawless, and grow in grace and knowledge; to him be glory now and to the day of eternity.

Paul is in chains in Rome and expects to die. He writes to Timothy at Ephesus to encourage him to stay faithful, pass on the teaching and come to him before winter. It is usually thought to be his last letter.
events.n: If Paul wrote it, the letter fits a second imprisonment in Rome after the end of Acts, and heavier than the rented house of Acts 28:30. Acts does not tell this part of his life. Early Christian writers say Paul was put to death in Rome under Nero (for example 1 Clement 5, c. AD 96). Some scholars think the three pastoral letters were written after Paul's death by someone using his name, and date 2 Timothy later.

events.sum: While everyone in Asia has deserted him, Paul remembers Onesiphorus, who "searched diligently until he found me" and "was unashamed of my chains."
Paul reminds Timothy that from infancy he has known the Holy Scriptures, and says Scripture is useful "for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness."
Paul says he is "already being poured out like a drink offering," that he has "finished the race" and "kept the faith," and that a crown of righteousness is laid up for him.

events.t: "No one stood with me": Paul's first defense
events.sum: At his first defense no one stood with Paul, but "the Lord stood by me and strengthened me." He trusts the Lord to bring him safely into His heavenly kingdom.
Paul, Peter, James, John and Jude write letters to guide the young churches.
Rome blames Christians for the great fire. Tradition says Peter and Paul died around this time.

events.t: Rome destroys Jerusalem and the Temple
events.sum: Roman armies burn the Temple, as Jesus had said.

An unnamed writer sends a "word of exhortation" to a tested community, arguing that God's final word came in his Son, who is greater than the angels, Moses and the Levitical priests, and urging the readers to hold on.
events.n: The letter names neither its author nor its readers. It was known in Rome by about AD 96, when 1 Clement quotes it, so it is older than that. It never mentions the destruction of the Temple, and the writer speaks of the priests and the sacrifices in the present tense; some scholars take that to mean that the Temple still stood (before AD 70), and others that the writer is describing the law in Scripture and not the Temple. Timothy has been released (13:23), which fits the time of Paul, but nothing else decides the date. The place is also unknown; "those from Italy" (13:24) may point to Rome.

events.t: The Son is greater than the angels
events.sum: God has spoken in his Son, the heir of all things and the radiance of his glory, who sat down at the right hand; the writer sets him above the angels, and warns the readers not to drift.

events.t: Today, if you hear his voice
events.sum: The writer sets Jesus above Moses and uses Psalm 95 to warn the readers not to harden their hearts as Israel did in the wilderness, since a rest still waits for the people of God.

events.t: A great high priest who sympathizes
events.sum: Jesus is a great high priest who has passed through the heavens and can deal gently with the weak, since he too was tested and learned obedience through what he suffered.

events.t: A priest in the order of Melchizedek
events.sum: The writer reads Genesis 14 and Psalm 110 to show that a priest like Melchizedek, with an oath and a life that cannot end, is greater than the Levitical priests.
The writer quotes Jeremiah 31:31-34, where God promises a new covenant written on the heart, and says that the first covenant is obsolete.

events.t: One sacrifice for sins, once for all
events.sum: Unlike the high priest who entered the inner room year after year, Christ entered once with his own blood, and having offered one sacrifice for sins, sat down.

events.t: By faith: the list of the faithful
events.sum: The writer defines faith and tells of Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham and Sarah, Moses, Rahab and many more who died without receiving what was promised.

events.t: Not Mount Sinai but Mount Zion
events.sum: The readers have come not to a mountain of fire and darkness but to Mount Zion, the city of the living God, and are receiving an unshakable kingdom.
Jesus suffered outside the city gate, and the writer asks the readers to go to him outside the camp, bearing his disgrace.

events.t: The first letter of John: what we have heard, seen and touched
events.sum: The writer opens with the Word of life, which he and others have heard, seen with their own eyes and touched with their hands, and proclaims it so that his readers will share fellowship with the Father and the Son and his joy will be complete.
events.n: The letter has no greeting, no name and no closing. Tradition from Irenaeus on ascribes it to John the apostle at Ephesus, late in the first century, and it is usually dated between about AD 85 and 100; some scholars place it earlier or later. Its link to the Gospel of John, in vocabulary and themes, is close, and the order in which they were written is debated.

events.t: God is light: walking in the light
events.sum: God is light and in Him there is no darkness at all. To claim fellowship with Him while walking in darkness is to lie; walking in the light brings fellowship with one another and the cleansing blood of Jesus.

events.t: If we confess our sins: an advocate and the atoning sacrifice
events.sum: To say we have no sin is to deceive ourselves, but if we confess, God is faithful and just to forgive. Jesus Christ the Righteous One is our advocate and the atoning sacrifice for the sins of the whole world.

events.t: How we know Him: keeping His commandments
events.sum: We know we have come to know Him if we keep His commandments; whoever claims to abide in Him must walk as Jesus walked.

events.t: An old commandment that is new: love your brother
events.sum: The command to love is old, because it was heard from the beginning, and new, because the true light is already shining. Whoever hates his brother is still in the darkness.

The writer tells each group why he writes: the children because their sins are forgiven and they know the Father, the fathers because they know Him who is from the beginning, the young men because they have overcome the evil one.
The desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes and the pride of life are not from the Father but from the world, which is passing away; whoever does the will of God remains forever.

events.t: It is the last hour: many antichrists
events.sum: Many antichrists have appeared. Some went out from the community, and the one who denies that Jesus is the Christ denies the Father and the Son.

events.t: The anointing from the Holy One: remain in Him
events.sum: The readers have an anointing from the Holy One that teaches them about all things; they are to remain in what they heard from the beginning and in the Son, so as to be unashamed when He appears.

events.t: Behold what manner of love: we are children of God
events.sum: The Father's love makes believers children of God now; what they will be has not been revealed, but when Christ appears they will be like Him, and this hope purifies.

events.t: Practicing righteousness, not sin: the works of the devil destroyed
events.sum: Christ appeared to take away sins and to destroy the works of the devil. Whoever is born of God does not go on sinning; the children of God and the children of the devil are told apart by righteousness and love.

events.t: Do not be like Cain: love and hatred
events.sum: The message from the beginning is that we should love one another, unlike Cain, who murdered his righteous brother. The world's hatred is no surprise; love is the sign of passing from death to life.

events.t: Jesus laid down His life: love in action and truth
events.sum: Love is known by Jesus laying down His life for us; believers ought to lay down their lives for the brothers, and share what they have with a brother in need.

events.t: God is greater than our hearts: confidence and the two commandments
events.sum: Whatever our hearts say, God is greater and knows all things. Keeping His commandments gives confidence in prayer; the commandment is to believe in the name of His Son and to love one another, and the Spirit shows that He remains in us.

Many false prophets have gone out into the world. The test of the Spirit of God is the confession that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh; greater is He who is in the readers than he who is in the world.

events.t: God is love: He sent His Son as the atoning sacrifice
events.sum: Love comes from God, and God is love. His love was revealed in sending His only Son so that we might live; no one has ever seen God, but if we love one another, God remains in us.

events.t: We have seen and testify: Savior of the world
events.sum: The Spirit he has given shows that God remains in us. The writer and others testify that the Father sent His Son to be the Savior of the world; whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God abides in God.
Love perfected gives confidence on the day of judgment, and perfect love drives out fear. We love because He first loved us, and whoever loves God must love his brother.

events.t: Born of God: the victory that has overcome the world
events.sum: Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ is born of God. Loving God means keeping His commandments, which are not burdensome, and our faith is the victory that has overcome the world.

events.t: Water, blood and the Spirit: three that testify
events.sum: Jesus Christ came by water and blood, and the Spirit, the water and the blood are in agreement. God's testimony is that He has given eternal life, and this life is in His Son.
events.n: What the water and the blood mean is debated. Many take them to be Jesus' baptism and death; others, His birth and death, or the water and blood from His side in John 19:34. The extra words in 5:7 about three that bear record in heaven, found in the King James Version, are not in the early Greek manuscripts.

events.t: That you may know you have eternal life
events.sum: The letter is written so that believers may know they have eternal life. They may have confidence that God hears what is asked according to His will, and may ask for a brother who sins a sin not leading to death.

events.t: We know: keep yourselves from idols
events.sum: The letter closes with three things we know: anyone born of God does not keep on sinning, we are of God while the whole world is under the evil one, and the Son of God has come and given understanding. Then, abruptly: "Little children, keep yourselves from idols."

events.t: The second letter of John: the elder to the chosen lady
events.sum: A letter of one chapter from “the elder” to “the chosen lady and her children,” whom he loves in the truth. The truth abides in us and will be with us forever, and grace, mercy and peace will be with us in truth and love.
events.n: The letter gives no name, no town and no date. Church writers from Irenaeus on quote it as the work of John the apostle, who is placed at Ephesus in his last years, and it is usually dated between about AD 85 and 100. Some scholars think “the elder” was a different John; the pages note both views. The “chosen lady” is most often read as a church.

events.t: Walking in the truth: the commandment from the beginning
events.sum: The writer is overjoyed to find some of the lady’s children walking in the truth. He asks that we love one another, a commandment we have had from the beginning, and says that love is walking according to His commandments.

events.t: Many deceivers: refusing to confess Jesus Christ in the flesh
events.sum: Many deceivers have gone out into the world, refusing to confess the coming of Jesus Christ in the flesh. Any such person is the deceiver and the antichrist.

events.t: Watch yourselves: do not lose what we have worked for
events.sum: The readers are told to watch themselves so that they do not lose what has been worked for, but are fully rewarded.

events.t: Remaining in the teaching of Christ
events.sum: Anyone who runs ahead without remaining in the teaching of Christ does not have God; whoever remains in it has both the Father and the Son.

events.t: Do not receive him into your home or even greet him
events.sum: A visitor who does not bring this teaching is not to be received into the home or greeted, because whoever greets such a person shares in his evil deeds. The verses are about teachers who bring a different teaching about Christ.
events.n: Traveling teachers depended on the hospitality of Christian homes, so refusing a welcome was a serious step. 3 John shows the opposite fault, where a leader will not receive the brothers. The Didache has rules for the same situation.

events.t: Paper and ink: face to face
events.sum: The writer has many things to say but would rather not use paper and ink; he hopes to come and speak face to face, so that their joy may be complete. The children of the readers’ chosen sister send greetings.

events.t: The third letter of John: the elder to the beloved Gaius
events.sum: A private letter from “the elder” to Gaius, whom he loves in the truth. He prays that Gaius may prosper in every way and enjoy good health, as his soul prospers.
events.n: The letter gives no name, no town and no date. It comes from the same elder as 2 John, whom early tradition calls John and places at Ephesus, and it is usually dated between about AD 85 and 100. Gaius is otherwise unknown; a list from about AD 380 makes a Gaius bishop of Pergamum, which cannot be checked. The health wish follows the custom of Greek letters.

events.t: No greater joy: my children are walking in the truth
events.sum: Brothers have come and testified about Gaius’s devotion to the truth. The elder has no greater joy than to hear that his children are walking in the truth.

events.t: Gaius and the strangers: fellow workers for the truth
events.sum: Gaius is faithful in what he does for the brothers, though they are strangers to him. They went out on behalf of the Name, accepting nothing from the Gentiles, so believers ought to support them and become fellow workers for the truth.
events.n: Traveling workers depended on Christian homes for food, a bed and help for the next stage of the road. 2 John sets the limit on the other side: a teacher who does not bring the teaching of Christ is not to be received.

events.t: Diotrephes, who loves to be first
events.sum: The elder has written to the church, but Diotrephes, who loves to be first, will not accept his instruction. He slanders the elder, refuses to welcome the brothers, forbids those who want to, and puts them out of the church.
events.n: The letter charges Diotrephes with ambition and with the way he treats people, not with false teaching. What position he held is debated.

events.t: Do not imitate what is evil, but what is good
events.sum: Gaius is told not to imitate what is evil but what is good. The one who does good is of God; the one who does evil has not seen God.

events.t: Demetrius: a good testimony from everyone
events.sum: Demetrius has a good testimony from everyone and from the truth itself, and the elder adds his own. He is probably the bearer of the letter.

events.t: Pen and ink: face to face, and peace
events.sum: The elder has much to write but would rather not use pen and ink; he hopes to see Gaius soon and speak face to face. He sends peace and the greetings of the friends, and asks Gaius to greet the friends by name.

events.t: The letter of Jude: a brother of James writes to those who are called
events.sum: Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and a brother of James, writes to those who are called, loved by God the Father and kept in Jesus Christ, and wishes them mercy, peace and love.
events.n: The letter names no place and no date. Most readers take Jude to be the Judas listed among the brothers of Jesus in Mark 6:3. Dates from the AD 50s to about AD 90 are proposed; if 2 Peter used Jude, Jude is the earlier of the two. Some scholars think it was written later in Jude’s name.

events.t: Contend for the faith: certain men have crept in
events.sum: Jude meant to write about the salvation he shares with his readers, but must urge them to contend for the faith entrusted once for all to the saints. Ungodly men have crept in who turn grace into a license for immorality and deny Jesus Christ.

events.t: Three warnings: the wilderness, the angels and Sodom
events.sum: Those delivered from Egypt who did not believe were destroyed; angels who left their proper dwelling are kept in chains for the judgment; Sodom and Gomorrah stand as an example.
events.n: The angels are most likely those of Genesis 6:1-4 as the Jewish Book of Enoch tells the story. 2 Peter 2:4-9 uses the same examples.

events.t: Michael and the devil dispute over the body of Moses
events.sum: The intruders defile their bodies, reject authority and slander glorious beings. Even the archangel Michael, disputing with the devil over the body of Moses, left the rebuke to the Lord.
events.n: The story is not in the Old Testament. Clement of Alexandria and Origen say it came from a Jewish book, the Assumption of Moses, whose ending is now lost.

events.t: Woe to them: Cain, Balaam and Korah
events.sum: They have taken the path of Cain, rushed into the error of Balaam, and perished in the rebellion of Korah.

events.t: Hidden reefs at the love feasts
events.sum: At the church’s shared meals these men look after only themselves. They are clouds without water, fruitless trees, wild waves and wandering stars.

events.t: Enoch’s prophecy: the Lord is coming with His holy ones
events.sum: Jude quotes Enoch, the seventh from Adam: the Lord is coming with myriads of his holy ones to judge everyone and convict the ungodly. These men grumble, follow their desires, boast and flatter.
events.n: The quotation is 1 Enoch 1:9, from a Jewish book outside the Old Testament. Copies of it were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls.

events.sum: The apostles warned that scoffers would come in the last times, following their own ungodly desires. These are the ones who cause divisions and do not have the Spirit.

events.t: Keep yourselves in the love of God; have mercy on those who doubt
events.sum: The readers are to build themselves up in their most holy faith, pray in the Holy Spirit, keep themselves in God’s love and wait for the mercy of Jesus Christ. They are to show mercy to doubters and snatch others from the fire.

events.t: To Him who is able to keep you from stumbling
events.sum: A closing hymn of praise to the only God our Savior, who is able to keep his people from stumbling and present them unblemished with great joy, through Jesus Christ our Lord.
The apostle John, exiled on Patmos, sees the risen Christ and is shown what will come.

events.t: The revelation of Jesus Christ is given to John
events.sum: God gives Jesus Christ a revelation to show his servants, and it is sent by an angel to John. John writes to the seven churches of Asia with grace and peace from God, from the seven Spirits and from Jesus Christ, the faithful witness.
events.n: Irenaeus, about AD 180, says the vision was seen near the end of Domitian’s reign, about AD 95. A minority of scholars date the book to the late 60s. The writer calls himself John; early tradition says he was the apostle.

events.t: John sees one like a son of man among seven lampstands
