events.sum: On Patmos, on the Lord’s day, John hears a voice like a trumpet and sees the risen Christ, with eyes like fire and a sword from his mouth, walking among seven golden lampstands. He is told to write what he sees.
A hard-working church that tests false teachers is told it has abandoned its first love.
A poor and slandered church is told not to fear what it is about to suffer: be faithful even unto death.
A church living where Satan’s throne is has held fast, though Antipas was killed, but some follow the teaching of Balaam.
A church growing in love and service tolerates a prophetess, called Jezebel, who leads believers into idolatry.
A church with a reputation for being alive is dead and must wake up; a few have kept their garments clean.
A church with little strength has kept Christ’s word and is given an open door that no one can shut.
A rich, lukewarm church is told it is poor, blind and naked. Christ stands at the door and knocks.

events.t: John sees the throne in heaven
events.sum: Through an open door John sees God enthroned, with twenty-four elders and four living creatures who never stop saying, “Holy, Holy, Holy.”

events.t: The Lamb takes the sealed scroll
events.sum: No one is worthy to open the scroll in God’s hand except the Lion of Judah, whom John sees as a Lamb that was slain. All heaven and every creature worship God and the Lamb.

events.t: John sees the seven seals opened
events.sum: The Lamb opens the seals: four horsemen, the souls under the altar, and the great day of wrath. Between the sixth and seventh, 144,000 are sealed and a countless multitude stands before the throne.
events.n: Christians differ on how these visions relate to history: as events of John’s own time, as the course of church history, as events still to come, or as pictures true of every age. The timeline’s “future” section follows the third reading.

events.sum: Six trumpets bring warning judgments on earth, sea, rivers, sky and mankind, yet people do not repent. John eats a little scroll, two witnesses prophesy and are killed and raised, and the seventh trumpet announces the kingdom of God.
events.n: Christians differ on how these visions relate to history: as events of John’s own time, as the course of church history, as events still to come, or as pictures true of every age. The timeline’s “future” section follows the third reading.

events.t: John sees the woman, the dragon and the two beasts
events.sum: A dragon tries to devour the Messiah, is thrown out of heaven and makes war on the woman’s children. A beast from the sea and a beast from the earth demand worship. The Lamb stands on Mount Zion with his people, and the earth is harvested.
events.n: Christians differ on how these visions relate to history: as events of John’s own time, as the course of church history, as events still to come, or as pictures true of every age. The timeline’s “future” section follows the third reading.

events.t: John sees the seven bowls of wrath
events.sum: Those who conquered the beast sing the song of Moses and the Lamb. Seven bowls are poured out, the kings gather at Armageddon, and a voice from the throne says, “It is done!”
events.n: Christians differ on how these visions relate to history: as events of John’s own time, as the course of church history, as events still to come, or as pictures true of every age. The timeline’s “future” section follows the third reading.

events.t: John sees the fall of Babylon the great
events.sum: A prostitute named Babylon sits on a scarlet beast and on seven hills. An angel announces her fall, and kings, merchants and sailors mourn the city that made them rich.
events.n: For John’s first readers Babylon pointed to Rome. Other readings take it as Jerusalem, as a power still to come, or as every proud city that sets itself against God.

events.t: John sees the rider on the white horse and the thousand years
events.sum: Heaven sings Hallelujah for the marriage of the Lamb. Christ rides out as King of kings; the beast and false prophet are destroyed; Satan is bound a thousand years, released and thrown into the lake of fire; and the dead are judged before the great white throne.
events.n: The thousand years are read as a future reign of Christ on earth after his return (premillennial), as the present age of the church (amillennial), or as a coming age of the gospel’s success before his return (postmillennial).

events.t: John sees the new heaven, the new earth and the new Jerusalem
events.sum: The first heaven and earth pass away. The holy city comes down from God as a bride, God dwells with his people and wipes away every tear, and the river and the tree of life are open to the nations.

Jesus says three times that he is coming soon. The Spirit and the bride say, “Come!” John warns against adding to or taking from the book and ends with a prayer and a blessing of grace, the last words of the Bible.
Believers who have died rise and those alive are gathered to the Lord. Christians differ on when this happens in relation to the tribulation.
events.n: Christians differ on the order and timing of these events. They are placed here in the order Revelation presents them.

events.sum: Jesus and Revelation describe a time of great distress, with seals, trumpets and bowls of judgment on the earth.
events.n: Christians differ on the order and timing of these events. They are placed here in the order Revelation presents them.

events.sum: The great city that opposes God and corrupts the nations is destroyed.
events.n: Christians differ on the order and timing of these events. They are placed here in the order Revelation presents them.

events.sum: Jesus returns in glory as King of kings. "This same Jesus... will come back in the same way you saw Him go."
events.n: Christians differ on the order and timing of these events. They are placed here in the order Revelation presents them.

events.sum: The beast and false prophet are defeated and thrown into the lake of fire.
events.n: Christians differ on the order and timing of these events. They are placed here in the order Revelation presents them.

events.sum: An angel binds Satan for a thousand years.
events.n: Christians differ on the order and timing of these events. They are placed here in the order Revelation presents them.

events.sum: Christ reigns with His people. Isaiah describes nations seeking God and a peace where the wolf lives with the lamb. Christians differ on whether this is literal, and when it happens.
events.n: Christians differ on the order and timing of these events. They are placed here in the order Revelation presents them.

events.sum: Satan is released, gathers the nations against God's people, and is defeated for good.
events.n: Christians differ on the order and timing of these events. They are placed here in the order Revelation presents them.

events.sum: The dead stand before God's throne and are judged. Death and Hades are thrown into the lake of fire.
events.n: Christians differ on the order and timing of these events. They are placed here in the order Revelation presents them.

events.t: A new heaven and a new earth
events.sum: God makes all things new. "The first heaven and the first earth had passed away."
events.n: Christians differ on the order and timing of these events. They are placed here in the order Revelation presents them.

events.sum: The New Jerusalem comes down from heaven to the new earth. "Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man."
events.n: Christians differ on the order and timing of these events. They are placed here in the order Revelation presents them.

events.sum: Isaiah pictures a renewed creation with no more weeping, long life and peace.
events.n: Christians differ on the order and timing of these events. They are placed here in the order Revelation presents them.

events.t: The river and tree of life
events.sum: The river of life flows from God's throne, the tree of life grows, and there is no more curse.
events.n: Christians differ on the order and timing of these events. They are placed here in the order Revelation presents them.

events.sum: God's servants see His face and reign with Him forever and ever.
events.n: Christians differ on the order and timing of these events. They are placed here in the order Revelation presents them.

eras.name: Creation and the early world
eras.sum: In the beginning: the Word, the seven days, Eden, the fall, the flood and the tower of Babel.

eras.name: The patriarchs
eras.sum: God calls Abraham and promises him a family and a land. Isaac, Jacob and Joseph carry the promise into Egypt.

eras.name: Exodus and the Law
eras.sum: God rescues Israel from slavery, gives the Law at Sinai and leads the people through the wilderness.

eras.name: The Promised Land
eras.sum: Israel enters the land under Joshua, then lives through the time of the judges.

eras.name: Kings and prophets
eras.sum: Saul, David and Solomon rule. The kingdom splits, and the prophets warn until Assyria and Babylon conquer.

eras.name: Exile and return
eras.sum: Judah is taken to Babylon, then returns under Persia to rebuild the Temple and the walls.

eras.name: Between the Testaments
eras.sum: Greek and Roman rule, the Maccabean revolt and Herod. No new biblical books are written.

eras.name: The life of Jesus
eras.sum: Jesus is born, teaches, heals, dies and rises again.

eras.name: The early church
eras.sum: The Spirit comes at Pentecost and the gospel spreads from Jerusalem to Rome.

eras.name: Things to come
eras.sum: Christ returns, the great judgment, and a new heaven and new earth where God lives with his people.

refs.name: 2 Peter and the rest of the Bible
refs.blurb: The second letter of Peter leans on the story of Israel and on Jude. The angels in chains, Noah and the flood, Sodom and Lot, Balaam and his donkey, and the dog and the sow come from Genesis, Numbers and Proverbs, and chapter 2 follows Jude 4-18 closely. The Transfiguration in the Gospels is the "holy mountain" of chapter 1, and the Day of the Lord, the thief, the new heaven and the new earth join Isaiah, Jesus' sayings, Paul, Hebrews and Revelation. Peter's last words sit beside Paul's in 2 Timothy 4, and the letter ends by naming Paul. Arrows follow the order of the books.

refs.name: 1 John and the rest of the Bible
refs.blurb: The first letter of John reads like the Gospel of John in a different key: the Word from the beginning, light and darkness, abiding, the new commandment, being born of God, the paraklētos and the Spirit of truth all come from it. The letter also reaches back to the Day of Atonement, to Cain and Abel and to the tests for a prophet in Deuteronomy, and answers teachers who denied that Jesus Christ had come in the flesh. 2 John and 3 John repeat its phrases, and Jude and Revelation echo its words. Arrows follow the order of the books.

refs.name: 2 John and the rest of the Bible
refs.blurb: The second letter of John packs the themes of the first and the Gospel into thirteen verses: truth, love, the commandment from the beginning, the coming of Jesus Christ in the flesh, remaining in the teaching, and joy that is complete. It also touches the practice of the house church and the care of travelers, which Acts, Romans and 3 John show from other sides, and the warnings against false teachers in Matthew, Acts and 2 Peter. Arrows follow the order of the books.

refs.name: 3 John and the rest of the Bible
refs.blurb: The third letter of John is a private note about hospitality and leadership. Its lines reach back to Abraham’s welcome of strangers and to the words of Jesus on receiving those he sends and on wanting to be first, and across to Acts, Paul and Hebrews on sending travelers on their way, commending a letter carrier and imitating what is good. Its closing words (testimony that is true, peace, friends, each by name) are those of the Gospel of John. The links with 2 John are drawn in the 2 John layer. Arrows follow the order of the books.

refs.name: Jude and the rest of the Bible
refs.blurb: Jude packs more of the Old Testament into 25 verses than almost any page of the New: Cain, Enoch, the angels of Genesis 6, Sodom, the Exodus, Korah, Balaam, the grave of Moses, Michael, and the high priest snatched from the fire in Zechariah 3. Lines run forward to Paul’s warnings about people who twist grace and about the last days, to the letter of James his brother, and to Revelation, where Michael, Balaam and the coming of the Lord with his armies appear again. The many links with 2 Peter 2 are drawn in the 2 Peter layer. Jude 14-15 quotes the Book of Enoch, which is not in the Bible and so has no line here. Arrows follow the order of the books.

refs.name: Revelation and the rest of the Bible
refs.blurb: Revelation never quotes the Old Testament with “it is written,” yet it echoes it in most of its verses, more than any other New Testament book. The lines here show the main sources: Genesis for the serpent and the tree of life; Exodus for the plagues, the lamb and the song by the sea; Isaiah for the new creation; Ezekiel for the throne, the scroll, Gog and the river; Daniel for the beasts, the son of man and the three and a half years; Zechariah for the horses and the olive trees. Other lines run to the words of Jesus about the end in Matthew 24 and Mark 13 and to the Gospel of John. The Bible’s first three chapters and its last three answer one another. Arrows follow the order of the books.
